newsitem.title: USA: U.S. finance reform bill unbalanced--SEC's Levitt.
newsitem.headline: U.S. finance reform bill unbalanced--SEC's Levitt.

text.p: The top U.S. securities regulator said Thursday a proposal before Congress to overhaul financial laws tilted excessively toward imposing bank regulation on securities firms.

Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Arthur Levitt said he backed the "primary goal" of the bill to break down the legal barriers separating banking from other financial activities like insurance and securities underwriting.
But, he told a House Commerce subcommitte that the current legislation needed to be reworked.

"Banking regulation, however, is not an adequate substitute for securities regulation, especially when a bank fully engages in a public securities business," Levitt said in prepared testimony. "Regrettably, (the bill) approaches financial services reform largely from a banking perspective."
Levitt opposed provisions of the bill giving the Federal Reserve a central role in overseeing diversified financial holding companies that own banks.

"It is unclear why, as contemplated in (the bill), a securities entity that functioned effectively without Federal Reserve Board umbrella regulation suddenly needs that regulation when it affiliates with a bank," Levitt said.

Fed chairman Alan Greenspan, also testifying on Thursday, defended the need for Fed oversight, however. Greenspan said the central bank could not effectively deal with systemic crises if it did not have oversight over major participants in the banking system.
Levitt said the bill also would not provide adequate protection for investors because different rules would apply to banks and securities firms selling securities.
